claims.claim: Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial rents for subdivided units.
A better reform is to strengthen tenure security and enforce habitability standards while lightly regulating initial rents.
A hard cap would harm the households it intends to protect.
SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium over mainstream flats.
Real rent burden for SDU tenants has worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income.
The poorest tenants have the least bargaining power in the SDU segment.
First-generation rent controls consistently cause supply contraction, while second-generation controls show small or null effects.
Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance is a second-generation control and SDU stock rose from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025.
Citing the 2021 ordinance's stock stability as evidence that more control is safe is a category error.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction would remove roughly 3 to 5 percent of SDU-type stock over five years.
A modelled 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about 900 dollars per month to incumbents.
A hard cap would leave 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment.
Berlin's Mietendeckel experience shows that suppressed increases release and new-contract rents jump above the pre-cap trend line.
Those excluded by a cap are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households, and public-housing waiters.
Current inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
A band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail of tenants.
The NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer.
The binding constraint for tenants is queue length and tenancy insecurity, not price.
A hard cap framed as deprivation of rental income would almost certainly attract compensation claims under the Basic Law.
The right package is statutory tenure security, mandatory written agreements, a light initial-rent band, and aggressive habitability enforcement.

cites.sentence: SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium over mainstream flats [D1p1], and real rent burden has worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income [D2p2].
SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium over mainstream flats [D1p1], and real rent burden has worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income [D2p2].

Mrs Wong, who has lived in an SDU for nine years without a written agreement, supports a cap because "the landlord still raises rent by whatever the market of desperate newcomers bears" [D4p1]–[D4p2].

Mrs Wong, who has lived in an SDU for nine years without a written agreement, supports a cap because "the landlord still raises rent by whatever the market of desperate newcomers bears" [D4p1]–[D4p2].
First-generation controls show consistent supply contraction; second-generation controls show small or null effects [D6p2].

Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance is second-generation, and the stock index confirms stability: estimated SDU stock rose from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025, continuing through the ordinance [D2p1].
This stability is often cited as evidence that more control is safe [D12p2]—but that reading is a category error.
The 2021 ordinance capped increases within existing tenancies while leaving initial rents untouched [D1p3].

A hard cap on initial rents is a different instrument, and the elasticity estimates for marginal SDU-type stock—0.31 to 0.48—imply that a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

A modelled 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about 900 dollars per month to incumbents, against 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].
Berlin illustrates the mechanism: when the Mietendeckel fell, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend line [D7p2].
The cap protects those already inside; the bill goes to those still outside [D7p3].
In Hong Kong, those outside are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households, and public-housing waiters [D1p2]—precisely the population the cap claims to serve.
Current inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].
The tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], or the newest arrivals.
Enforcement would therefore systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].
The subcommittee could not identify any design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].
He names the waiting list" [D3p3].
The NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1].
Rent caps treat the price symptom of a quantity problem [D11p2].
Every unit of enforcement capacity spent policing rents is a unit not spent inspecting fire, partition, and ventilation conditions, where harm is documented and immediate [D11p2].

A hard cap framed as deprivation of rental income would almost certainly attract compensation claims under the Basic Law; a contractual-term regulation sits on firmer ground but leaves initial rent unregulated [D9p1].
A middle instrument—a published, indexed per-square-foot band—could be defended as rate-capping rather than confiscation, but requires survey infrastructure that does not exist [D9p2].

This addresses the insecurity Mr Chan describes—the landlord who ended his tenancy with two weeks' notice [D3p1]—without triggering the contraction that would close the door on the next family in the queue.
The 2021 ordinance showed that light regulation can coexist with stable stock [D2p1].
